newsitem.title: UK: German government bonds to lose out if U.S. rates.
newsitem.headline: German government bonds to lose out if U.S. rates.

text.p: Investors should look to U.S. Treasuries rather than German government bonds over the next few weeks, despite market expectations for higher U.S. interest rates, analysts said on Tuesday.
The Federal Open Market Committee meets to decide interest rate policy on March 25, and many market players anticipate a 25 basis point rise in the current Fed funds rate of 5.25 percent.
"In the U.S. the markets remain bearish. But a lot of bad news is priced in," said Kirit Shah at Sanwa International. "So if the Fed does tighten, the yield spread will continue fall."
At 1151 GMT, the 10-year T-note/Bund gap was at 94 basis points having narrowed from 114 in early March.

"The spread is going to remain in a volatile band between 80 to 115," said chief market strategist Shah, in London. "Bunds are in a supportive trend but vis a vis the U.S. they are still underperforming."
Adrian Schmidt, international economist at Chase in London, also saw the U.S./German gap narrowing.

"If there is a 25 basis point rise in the funds rate that may actually help to stabilise the T-bond market slightly even though that is not the typical result of a rate rise, particularly the first of a cycle," he said.

"It is so well anticipated this time round and the Fed is likely to add a rider that it is a very pre-emptive, and it will be seen as such. Given that is the case, it is possible that it will relieve some of the tension in the market."

By contrast, analysts said Bunds were dogged by concerns over Germany's ability to meet the three percent deficit target set out in the Maastricht Treaty and the possiblity of a delay to the start date for European Economic and Monetary Union.

"Although in theory Germany might get some support from talk of EMU delay, it is actually creating concerns that there might be easier fiscal policy if such a delay did happen which would be negative for the Bunds," said Schmidt.
The market was also taking German social problems, such as strikes and high unemployment, into consideration.
"That is leading to curve steepening which is certainly affecting the long end," Shah said "Bunds are not going to get much support until the six percent yield.
The benchmark 10-year Bund is currently at 100.80, yielding 5.88 percent.
Shah said he favoured a strategy of switching out of the German short end and into short dated U.S. Treasuries.

"On a global portolio basis shortening durations remains the best defensive posture," he said. "The U.S. short end has priced in quite a bit of tightening now. Two year yields are at 6.20 percent and could go to six and a quarter now."
But some analysts pictured a reverse senario with the T-note/Bund gap widening.
A strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said not only was the Fed likely to tighten monetary policy next week, but this would be followed by a further tightening in May.

"We would expect the U.S. to underperform over the next few weeks, with higher yields in the U.S. which will not be matched by increasing yields in Germany," he said. "So the spread will widen to around 125 basis points."
